title: Ribollita
subtitle: Tuscan bread and bean soup
excerpt: The great Tuscan peasant soup: a thick, deeply savoury broth of cannellini beans, cavolo nero, and root vegetables thickened with stale bread and poured over more bread to serve. The name means reboiled; it tastes better reheated the next day.

recipe.sourceNotes: Ribollita (the word means reboiled) is the defining soup of Tuscan peasant cooking, made to use up the minestrone and bean soup left from the previous days by reheating it with the addition of stale bread, which thickens and enriches the broth until it is almost solid. The dish is a paradigmatic example of cucina povera, the poor kitchen that turns yesterday's leftovers into today's best meal. The canonical version uses cannellini beans (which were historically the principal legume of Tuscany, before being partly displaced by fagioli borlotti), cavolo nero (black kale, the long-leafed Tuscan brassica), stale unsalted Tuscan bread, and olive oil. It is always served by ladling the soup over a slice of bread at the bottom of each bowl and finishing with a thread of raw olive oil.

content.text: The bread should be stale and without salt if possible: Tuscan bread (pane sciocco) is traditionally unsalted. Mash roughly a third of the beans before adding them to thicken the broth. The finished soup should be very thick, almost porridge-like. Finish with a generous pour of your best extra-virgin olive oil; it is part of the dish, not decoration.

items.preparation: 2 tins, drained and rinsed; or 350 g dried, soaked and cooked
stale; half broken into the soup, half sliced to serve

content.text: Heat the olive oil in a large pot over medium heat. Cook the onion, carrot, and celery for 10 minutes until soft. Add the garlic, thyme, and bay leaves and cook for 2 minutes. Add the tinned tomatoes and cook for 5 minutes.

Mash roughly a third of the cannellini beans with a fork. Add all the beans (mashed and whole) to the pot along with 1.5 litres of water, the cavolo nero, salt, and pepper. Bring to a simmer and cook for 40 minutes until the cavolo nero is very tender and the soup is thick.

Break the stale bread into rough chunks and stir into the soup. Cook for a further 20 minutes, stirring often, until the bread has completely dissolved into the broth and the soup is very thick. Remove the bay leaves. Taste and adjust the seasoning. Place a slice of bread in the base of each bowl, ladle the ribollita over it, and finish with a generous pour of extra-virgin olive oil.
